utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are the interpreters all ready? Good morning, is everybody ready? Does the Defence hear, does the Prosecutor hear? General Blaskic, do you hear? MR.. BLASKIC: Good morning, your Honour, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can then resume our work. Perhaps before beginning, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to say that we can set up a status conference for Friday, 28th, in the morning. We will set the hour, perhaps 9.30 for example, and the conference will deal with certain points which are still pending before us. First of all, is the 28th, Friday, a good date for you? There will not be a hearing on the 28th, therefore we could devote the morning to the status conference. I know that for my colleagues, this would be a good date. Would it be suitable for the Prosecutor, for the Defence? Mr. Nobilo, Mr. Hayman? The date is all right, all right. This is a status conference which would allow us, once the elections of the judges are completed and the constitution of the Trial Chambers has been renewed, would allow us to discuss among ourselves in camera to take measures for various issues which are arising. There are issues that have to do with scheduling, others for the two applications which are still pending, one on the review of the decision on the testimony -- whether the exculpatory statements, whether they have been accepted. There is also the request from the Defence on indirect testimony, hearsay evidence. There are all these questions which have to do with the subpoena which now can no longer be called a subpoena, which is the result of the decision of the Appeals Chamber. Therefore we also have to see how all of this is going to be dealt with again. Then there are scheduling issues in order to shorten the proceedings, which we asked you to think about, and to suggest things that we might do, measures that we might take that might be practical before the Trial Chamber takes a decision which might be necessary. These are all the issues. There is also the issues of substance which are much more important, substantive issues having to do with relations there might be between this case of General Blaskic, but possibly other trials which deal with the same acts that took place in the Lasva Valley. As you know, they are relevant since the arrest of a certain number of persons who are assumed guilty, and I say that they are assumed to be guilty. These are all of the questions which we may deal with on the 28th, Friday, in the morning, starting at 9.30. If there are no other comments, we could then continue. I see that Mr. Harmon will continue now for the following witness, and the Registrar has told me that there was perhaps a problem when it would come to reading the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning Mr. President, good morning your Honours, good morning counsel. The next witness the Prosecution calls is Ms. Fatima Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please tell me your name and your first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahmic Fatima.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to read a declaration to you and you would tell us if you agree with the statement. Perhaps it is a bit difficult for you to read. The Registrar might read it for you. Would you read the declaration for her?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I could read it and then it would be repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, and the witness will repeat it. The Registrar is going to read a declaration which is an oath which every witness must take. The Registrar will read it and you repeat it after him, please. MS. FATIMA AHMIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated now, ma'am. Ms. Ahmic, you have come here at the request of the Prosecution. I believe that the Prosecutor explained to you how everything would take place. First we would ask you to relax, you are sitting before judges who will listen to you. Do not be afraid, you have nothing to fear, nothing will happen to you. The Prosecutor will simply ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not afraid of anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then the counsel for General Blaskic will also ask you some questions. All of this I am sure has already been explained to you. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you can begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me begin by asking you some questions. How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 63 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you born and raised in the village of Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Loncari is a small village that is a few kilometres away from Ahmici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, when you were 19 years old, did you get married to your husband, your late husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you move from the village of Loncari to the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I married my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you and your husband eventually build a house in the section of Ahmici known as Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, were you living in the house that you and your husband built?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, what was your late husband's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, how old was Hasim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was born in 1951, I think he was 63 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he working or was he retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he do before his retirement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean what he did at work?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked in his enterprise in the Zenica steel works.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April 1993, did he have a serious medical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court what that medical condition was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had health problems with his kidneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did those health problems limit his daily activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he could only do small errands, he could not do any hard work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, I am going to show you a picture, if I could have the assistance of the usher in placing Prosecutor's Exhibit 127 on the ELMO. Ms. Ahmic, to your right there is a picture that appears on the ELMO and it may appear in front of you on the television screen. First of all, who is in that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband Hasim and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that picture taken in front of the house that you and your husband built in the Zume section of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately when was that picture taken, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was about ten years ago at the most, seven or eight years ago. I cannot tell you exactly. Ten years at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again with the assistance of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The picture, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct. With the assistance of the usher, if I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 110/4 placed on the ELMO as well? Mr. Usher, I am interested in the top picture. Ms. Ahmic, do you recognise that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who is in that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband -- this is my husband Hasim, this is my granddaughter Aida and this is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that picture taken, Ms. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 12 or 13 years ago. Sorry, 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move to admit Prosecutor's Exhibit 127 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, is this 127?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this is Exhibit 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, on 16th April 1993, was your husband in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would stand guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What exactly would he do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. He would just stand guard from time to time when they would ask him to. When this TO was established, you know, then they would go together to stand guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would he do that very often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he was told to go, he went. It depends whether he was healthy, whether he was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, on 16th April 1993, did you have any guns or other type of weapons in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many children do you have, Ms. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had three, they killed my son Fahrudin and now I have a daughter Saima and a son Nevzudin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your son Fahrudin build a house next to your house in Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How far away was his house from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten metres away, not more than that. It was right next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was Fahrudin married and did he have children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was married, he had three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, how old were his three children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that Aida, that is what I said then, I do not remember exactly, but Aida went to second grade, Semin and Emir did not go to school then. One of them was perhaps eight and the other one five, and the little one, Emir, was six -- I do not remember what years they were born in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did your son Fahrudin do for a living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son Fahrudin worked in Princip, which was a military company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He worked in the factory as a manager, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a manager in his enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he also a musician and did he play music to support his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when they were building their house, he worked extra, he played the drums, he played the guitar. He also had an accordion. He would only play the accordion at home, but he would play the guitar, he would play drums and he had all these instruments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, was Fahrudin a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he do, to your knowledge, in the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would say who would stand guard when and he would say who was supposed to go. That is what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Ms. Ahmic, on 16th April 1993, did Fahrudin have any weapons in his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Fahrudin had weapons, but you want me to tell you what kind of weapons he had?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had weapons. In the village of Slemenje there was some kind of barracks and the Serbs burned down the big barracks. They went to collect the parts of various weapons, so out of five or four rifles, they would make a single rifle. Drago Josipovic helped my son make a new rifle. A month or two afterwards, Nenad Santic took away this rifle from him and he gave it to Drago Josipovic and Drago Josipovic carried this rifle of his. They took away all our weapons, not only from my son, all our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that following the events in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere in between, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Between the attack in April and the previous attack in October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned, Ms. Ahmic, somebody by the name of Drago Josipovic. Drago Josipovic was your neighbour and he was a Croat, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drago Josipovic was my next door neighbour, there was only a fence between our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He was a Croat, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Nenad Santic. Nenad Santic was a Croat as well, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So sometime between April and October, I should say October and April, Nenad Santic ordered that guns in the possession of your son and other Muslims be turned in, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You personally observed your son turn over to Drago Josipovic the rifle that had been made from many different parts of other rifles, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I happened to be at my son's house and somebody rang at the door and my son was told that Nenad came to see him, so my son went out and he said, "Nenad asked me to hand in my rifle", so he gave him his rifle and Drago Josipovic then carried this rifle of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you to focus your attention on 15th April 1993, the day before the attack. Were you watching television on 15th April 1993, Ms. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see a television programme in which Tihomir Blaskic and Dario Kordic were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please tell the judges what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sitting there with my husband, we were drinking coffee, it was 3.00. From 3.00 until 3.30 there was not always a programme from Busovaca. My husband said, "please turn on the TV", I turned on the TV and we saw their army, you know, the Croat army. They were walking around and all of a sudden that disappeared, and all of a sudden you can see a room this big in Busovaca. Tihomir Blaskic was on television and Kordic, and a woman. Tihomir Blaskic said the following, "in the village of Ahmici, our soldiers were attacked", he said. Did I spoil something hear? I cannot hear anything, you know, now, in my headphones. I cannot hear this voice, you know. It may be something went wrong here. Maybe I did something wrong. Sorry, I did something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I hear you. Repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You had just described what Tihomir Blaskic said on the television programme. Can you continue your description of that programme, Ms. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. He said, "our soldiers were attacked in the village of Ahmici at the bungalow". This Blaskic then went silent and he had some kind of book in his hands like a book, you know, something like this, a paper, and he said, "we have nothing to talk about to them any more. We are not going to talk, we are only going to wage war. We are just waiting for our orders". All of a sudden, we were terrified, my husband and I. We thought something really went wrong. Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, who said that? Was that Blaskic or was that Kordic who said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kordic said that they were waiting for orders and that they would attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who said "it"? Could the Prosecutor clarify as to all the statements the witness has recounted, who said "it"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was attempting to do that, Mr. President, and if counsel does not like the term "it" I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, what do you mean by your objection? First of all, could you explain what your objection is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor used a term that was vague, your Honour, "who said that?". I would ask that it be clarified, is it only referring to the immediate statement which was, "we are waiting for our orders", or does it apply to the entire narrative that the witness has attributed to a speaker on the television programme. I would kindly ask the Prosecutor to clarify that for us all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It was a clarification that was being sought. That was the point. All right, Mr. Harmon. Would you please give us that clarification by having the objection repeated? We can see that it is being much more calmly -- when you object to something, please explain what it is that you are objecting to. Therefore please ask the witness more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, can you please explain what Dario Kordic said on that television programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic said the following, "we will not negotiate or talk to them any more. We are only waiting for our orders and that is it". Then the next morning they attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your reaction to seeing that television programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How should we have reacted? We did not sleep all night. We saw that something dangerous was going on, that something dangerous was being prepared. Since he stated that on television -- may I say this? My son Fahrudin came around 10.00 also and he said, "father, did you watch the Busovaca television?". He said, "yes". He said, "father, the same tape was shown in Vitez just as in Busovaca. I just saw it". I told him in a raised voice, "son, why did you come to tell me this now? I am getting ready to go to sleep. Go back and be with your family. You have no bad relationship with anybody, with the Croats".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, I would like to turn your attention to the morning of 16th April 1993. Were you and your husband at home on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the judges what happened that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That morning it happened around 5.30, I heard a large detonation, I was sleeping in the room and he was sleeping in the kitchen because he was ill, he liked it where it was warm. Then I heard this detonation and then I related it to what had happened on television the previous day, and then I said, "okay, it is starting, they are attacking us". Then downstairs the toilet was separate from the bathroom and I looked -- went into the toilet and I looked and I wanted to alert my son to get the children out. I could not see him. As I was looking through the window, they were coming out of Drago Josipovic's house and walking towards my house. As I was standing at the window, a Croat appeared and he told me at the window, he said, "do not budge, just stay where you are", and I did. Then they asked me, "where are your sons?" I said, "this is my son's house, that is my only son". "Where is your husband?", "here he is, he is in bed". They said, "do not budge, just stay where you are". Then they started breaking down the fence. It was house to house, so that was the fence separating. Then they broke down the fence and they positioned themselves on the corners of the house, at the corners. Then when I looked, one of them took a hand grenade and threw it in a small room at my son's. It was like a pantry, and I immediately ran into the room and I told my husband, "Hasim, dear, something is going on, something dangerous is going on at Fahran's", that is my son's nickname, "they threw a grenade into the house". We came and sat down on the edge of the sofa and we were saying what is going to happen to Fahran, what is going to happen to the children. Meanwhile I am hearing the shooting going around his house. I never thought about what would happen, that something like this would happen. But somehow I thought nothing would happen to him. Three or four minutes later, they threw a grenade into my bedroom upstairs. When it threw, the whole house shook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, let me interrupt you here for just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say that you saw people coming out of the yard of Drago Josipovic, were those HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were their faces covered or uncovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were uncovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. What happened after they threw a hand grenade into your house? Would you continue telling the judges what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We just remained seated, one next to another. I did not unlock the door, and they came and kicked the door rather forcefully a couple of times. We kept silent, we did not respond and they shouted, "come out, fuck your balija mothers, did I not tell you not to budge from the window?". I could see as they were kicking the door, they could not kick it in. They broke the automatic rifle on the lock. As they shot at the door, the door fell in and they said, "come out, fuck you, did I not tell you not to budge from there?". I came out and I shouted at them, "what is the matter? What do you want? Call Drago, call Miro, call Luca and ask them what neighbours we are, how we live with them". "I do not want to ask those questions", he said, "call your husband out and you go back into the house". There were three next to him and they pushed me back in. They had a plastic bottle of sorts, and there was like a spray and they started spraying the curtains and the sofa. He sent me back in and he called my husband out. As I looked and I told him, "come out, they are calling you". He came out and he was shaking like this, he could not make a step. I said, "come out, they are calling you". Then when he came out, he said, "stand against this pillar". As I looked, he took the rifle and he pointed like this and he said that he would kill him and I jumped, ran from the window and I embraced the soldier and I said, "do not kill him", and I was crying "be alive", and so he said he felt pity and he almost dropped his gun. I had a feeling that he was about to drop his gun. Then he said, "go". I said, "where do I go?". He said, and I apologise, he said, "go fucking wherever you want". We went to my son's house, it is ten metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, let me interrupt you for a minute. These soldiers who were confronting your husband with a gun, were they also dressed in camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw one soldier spraying a liquid on your curtains and on your sofa. Did you see what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he took a lighter and then he started lighting the curtain, and in several spots on the sofa. I saw that, but I came out to see what was going on with my husband and they stayed in there and they set it on fire and then it started burning. As I told him, "do not kill him, may you live forever", and they stayed in the house and I just wanted to take my slippers, but the soldier said, "do not take them, you will not need them". So we started towards my son's house, my husband and I. I did not know whether they were going to kill my husband from the back and I wanted to defend him, and so I started and I spread my arms like this so that I would protect him (indicates). When we arrived at my son's house, the children were screaming as if they were putting them on fire. I said, "please, I have a daughter-in-law and I have a son here, I want to see what is going on with them". I knocked on the door and my daughter-in-law opened the door, and meanwhile they called my son out. There were three doors to the house, there was a glass door and then they were going there and they called him through that door. So I entered the house and the children were screaming and I said, "what is going on?". My daughter-in-law said, "they are going to kill my children" and I said "no, no". Meanwhile the soldier behind me keeps nudging me with the barrel into my back. I said, "where is Fahran?". The little one said, "they killed father". I said "where?", and he said, "look down at the door". When I came to the door, I saw him down lying, he was dead, and I yelled, "my son Fahran, what did they do to you?". He told me, "look at him now, I will shoot your eyes now you have seen him. I did not shoot him, it is Alija who shot him. Look at him now". I wanted to look at him again and he said, "get away from here". Again he cursed my balija mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, how was your son dressed when you saw his body on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had like a blue work smock and he had jeans as far as I recall, and shoes, and I was so frightened, I could not see well. I was as if in a coma, you know, when you see your own child lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher in placing Prosecutor's Exhibit 128 on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, I will also be referring to 110/4 as well. Do you see the picture, Ms. Ahmic, on the television monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it. My son. Look what they did. How could they do something like this? How could they have killed him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have many other pictures that you want to show?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic -- Mr. Usher, could you place one more photograph on the ELMO, please? That would be 110/4, the lower picture on that two photo page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you like to rest for a few moments, Ms. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I rested, thank you. I am not going to have rest until I am dead. They killed my son and he was innocent. He was good with everyone. He had best friends among Croats, he played music with them, he went to school with them, he worked with them, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you wish to continue? Do you feel able to continue, Ms. Ahmic? Would you like us to suspend the hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecutor still has another photo to show you. Are you going to show that immediately, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is on the ELMO, but it does not appear on the screen, Mr. President, I am not sure if we are having a technical problem. I will identify it, Mr. President, it has been presented before, photograph 110/4. Ms. Ahmic, do you see the photograph at the bottom, with the young man and the woman. Is that also your son Fahrudin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my son Fahrudin, this is Fahrudin's wife Suada. This is my darling son.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you finished with the photographs, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Ms. Ahmic, can I continue asking you some questions, or do you need a couple of minutes of quiet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you like us to take a five minute break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am a bit ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, we will begin again at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing. Ms. Ahmic, do you feel a bit better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have courage. We will try to concentrate your questions, focus things. Do not make this distress last too long. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, did you eventually leave the house of your son Fahrudin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did you leave with and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went down towards -- down a field, the nearest house -- I was thinking of going to the house of Zarko and I went through the field, the door was open, I looked inside, I cannot recall now -- Carlo. Carlo was shooting from the hallway to the Ahmic Mekrema's house and I went towards the house and he closed the door. I knocked on the door because I wanted to save the children and so that we could stay in this house, so we would be protected from the shooting. Nobody opened, then I went to the next house, it was Ljuban's and I heard and the house was also full there, but they would not open it for me. Then we went down the field towards the Lasva, that is the name of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, let me interrupt you for just a moment. While you were going toward the Lasva river, did you turn around and look back at your son's house, and what was its condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I turned around, the flames were already coming out of the windows, you see it had been set on fire, the house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we started down towards, down the field -- my husband was carrying a child, my daughter-in-law was carrying a child, they were in pyjamas, they would not let us put on some shoes or bootees on them, they just said, "go, go, go" and I said, "where do I go? Tell me where to go?". They said, "go wherever you want, go to Alija, fuck him", so we went down and Drago was coming out of the woods, there was some fence and Anto Papic was there too. I started weeping, "dear Drago, why did you not save my Fahran?" He tells me -- he approached me to give me condolences. I said, "why do I need your condolences when you did not save my Fahran? Do you know who killed my Fahran?". He answered, "I do not know who killed him. I did not kill him". "Do you know who killed him?". "It was the force majeure who ordered it. The orders came from above", that is how he said. "I could not save him, I did not dare save him, I did not kill him". Then I yelled, "you know who killed him".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then what happened, Ms. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Since they came from your yard, the military did, you could know who killed my son", and he said, "I do not know who killed him". That is when he told me that the orders came from above. Then I asked him to go and sort of cover him so that the body would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are talking about Drago Josipovic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then what happened, Ms. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked Drago Josipovic where to go to save my children, and he said, "I do not know". Then I asked Anto Papic, "can we please go to your house Anto?", and he said, "I am in danger too". Drago Josipovic then said, "however, your house is in the woods. Let them be in your house", and that is where we stayed, in his house the entire day and that night, we also spent in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were at that house, Ms. Ahmic, did you leave that house and return to go back in the direction of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I left the children down there and my husband and I started up the field towards my son's. I thought maybe he was just wounded and I could still save him. Nikola's house was there and next to the house there were Croats, they were all armed and they were standing by the fence and they would not let me pass. They said, "where are you going?". "I want to see if my son was only wounded and then I can save him". They would not let me go so I had to go back down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, you said there were some Croats there. Approximately how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not count them, maybe 12, 13 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were they wearing, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember, it was all camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then did you return to Anto Papic's house and spend the night of the 16th at Anto Papic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me clarify one point with you, Ms. Ahmic. The person who said that orders came from above, was that Drago or was that Anto?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Drago who told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me turn your attention to the next morning, 17th April 1993. Can you tell the judges what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they first attacked us, is that it? When we were attacked for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, on the morning of the 17th. The night of the 16th you spent the night in Anto Papic's house. What happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning Anto came and Drago Josipovic came several times and they were saying Razim was killed, Asim, Munib, they counted about 20 people by their names. Drago Josipovic was the one who counted who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They were referring to Muslims, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims who were killed, yes. I shouted, "dear Drago, what is this? What is going on? Why are they killing all the Muslims here and torturing everything?" He also then, "I do not know, I did not order this, I did not order these killings". That is what Drago told me when I asked him. When I asked him, "why is it that people are being killed when all these neighbours were named?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Drago and Anto both came again and they said, "you Hasim and you Zenur and you Amir are going to be carrying the corpses into Ramiz's back yard". I said, "Hasim cannot carry the bodies. He is sick and he cannot take that". Then he said, "you Zenur and you Amir and Munib Heleg", he was there, "they will be carrying corpses to Ramiz's yard", and they went there. We stayed there until about 3.00 and Drago and Anto Papic came again and said, "get ready, you are going to go to be exchanged". "Where?", "to Zenica, you will be exchanged in Zenica". We started -- there were several families there in Anto Papic's house, there were about five or six families who spent the night there and we took the main road and so these people, my neighbours who spent the night there, and we went up a field to see whether our son had been carried away. When we arrived in front of the house, he had been carried away, there was only a big puddle of blood where he had been killed. My house was completely burned. When we came to his house, it was all burnt, and a pipe had burst from the heat, and so that prevented the top floor from burning completely. Then we took a bag and we climbed upstairs to take some clothes, we took a couple of coats, so that we would be warm. Then we left the house, so now he is going around the house and he is trying to feed the chicken. I said, "Hasim, they have all left, we are alone, let us go". Drago Josipovic was standing in his yard and I am asking him, "Drago, please, could Hasim and I stay in this summer kitchen?". It had not burnt. He said, "for all I know, you can stay, but the others will come and kill you". Then I was telling my husband, "come on, come on", and he was still closing the garage, the shed, and I was walking and I looked at the entrance gate as he was closing the gate and he had the bag with him and I was going up the road and there was towards Ramiz's house and there was a van. They all had black uniforms, these Croats were in the van. As I passed them, they did not say anything to him. I met Nikica Slikica who was coming down and I asked him -- he had a stocking over his head, but I recognised him. I asked him -- I said, "Hasim is coming, please just keep an eye on him so that nobody would say anything to him". Covic was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, let me direct your attention to the van that you passed that had people with black uniforms in it. Did you hear any of those people talking in the van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three people in black uniforms standing by the van and one of them had a walkie-talkie, and he had the antenna pulled out a little bit, and he was saying into the walkie-talkie, "yes, the operation was successful, they are lying in front of houses like pigs". My husband passed the van and they stopped him, they asked him where he was going and he said his name was Hasim Ahmic and he said they all went to Ljiljo's shop near the Pican's cafe. "What is in the bag?". "I am carrying some stuff for the children, my son was killed yesterday and I have three grandchildren, I am taking some clothing". He also had a blanket over his arm and they said, "come on, we will come for you, you will come with us to have coffee". He came to this room, I was in one corner and he told me, "they will come for me". I said "who?", "the ones from the van, did they tell you anything?". I said "no". "They told me they will come for me now".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it you and your husband then arrived at the shop where other Muslims were being detained, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was full of Muslims, it was like -- it was a store, a shop, so it was also like a storage room there and that is where we spent the night, and he comes to me and he says --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that where your husband explained to you what the men had said to him in the van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Papic came here, sat down and he says, "dear Fatima, they will come for me now". I said, "who?", "those from the van". I said, "do not worry, do not be afraid, take off your cap, maybe they will not recognise you". That is what he did, he took off his cap. Minutes later, three or four men arrived -- there were at least three, I do not know if there were four, but I am sure there were three at least. As he was sitting, he pointed the finger and he said, "you, old man, get up". Munib Heleg was standing there and he said, "you too". Zenur and Amir were among the children and the women and they sort of ducked as if they were hiding. Then this one said, "what are you doing there? You two, get up and come along with us". They got up. When my husband got up, he was shaking like this, he could not, and I also got up, and I said, "please do not. He is old, he is my husband, do you know that he is going to dialysis?", and they said, "he is going to get a dialysis right now", that is what they said. He just pushed me like this, I was holding a rifle and he just pushed me like this with it and I went back. Then they took them down towards Mujo's house. That is where they took them and I remained silent and there was a burst of fire. The house was burnt and there was a barn next to it and a little while later, the barn was aflame. Nikica Slikica was going there and I called him over and said, "please Nikica, come over and tell me, where did they take them, the three of them?". He approached, "they took them for some exchange". I said, "please Nikica, tell me the truth, what happened to them? Do not hide it from me. You know that I was friendly with your mother Mara, I swear with your dead mother"; "since you did that, just the order came and they were killed, just do not ask about that".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, let me clarify a couple of points of your testimony. First of all, in the transcript that I saw on the screen next to me, it said that Anto Papic came and sat down next to you and said, "they are going to come for me". In fact it was your husband saying "they", referring to the men --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was saying this, but Anto Papic was sitting there when my husband told me this, Anto Papic got up and he went to ask some women to get some milk for the children, and then five minutes later, these men came and took these -- the four of them out and went to Mujo Dedic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, were the men who came to get your husband and take him out, were those men the same men or different men that you had seen earlier in the combi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in the camouflage uniforms, they were not in black uniforms. The ones who came for my husband -- the ones in the van were in black uniforms and the ones that came for my husband and for Amir and Zenur and Munib, they were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Since April 17th 1993, have you ever seen your husband alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Munib Heleg alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Amir and Zenur Ramic alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me very quickly show you three photographs and ask you if you can identify the people and with the assistance of the usher, if I could have photographs 121 and 110/5 placed on the ELMO for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I was going to intervene on behalf of my colleagues for the following witness. The three of us have conferred and decided from now on, when there are emotional things happening, which might be, we would like you to turn to the Defence and to state what your intention is, that is as far as the tendering of exhibits goes. If there is no opposition from the Defence, they could be put into evidence immediately without having to go through the Defence. I was going to wait until the next witness in order to explain this position of the judges. If the Defence thinks that he wants to raise objections, at that point but only that point we will show the photographs to the witness. I thought that you were going to show other types of photographs, I suppose that these are also photographs of members of the families, Ms. Ahmic's family that is. You are the only one who can tell us. If these things are too emotional, please tell the Defence what they are and if necessary, show them to him and then we can put them into evidence. If not, we do not have to show them to the witness. We will do this for all the witnesses, whether they are Defence or Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not believe -- these photographs are photographs of the three men who were taken out along with her husband on the morning of 17th April 1993, Munib Heleg, Amir Ramic and Zenur Ramic, and she will testify that those individuals in the pictures that will be presented to her are those individuals who were taken out. I do not believe the reaction will be similar to what occurred earlier, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, show them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me start with 121, Ms. Ahmic, the single picture, Mr. Usher. I am sorry, that is not the picture that -- yes, Mr. Usher, that is the picture right there. Ms. Ahmic, before you is 110/5, is that a picture that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is Zenur and this is Amir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The two men in the picture are Zenur and Amir Ramic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, two brothers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to 121, can you tell me who is in that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Munib Heleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Ahmic -- Mr. Usher, I am finished with the pictures, thank you. Ms. Ahmic, why did you leave the shop on the morning of 17th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to us and they said, "go now wherever you want" and we said, "where are we to go?" Then they stood there and -- I do not know, they were talking something over and then they said, "come out and line up", and we all came out of that room, it was a big column that formed, there was women who were pregnant among us, and then he said, "you will be going with Nikica", so Nikica was going ahead and we went along the road towards the railroad station, and there they said, "stop, wait here". Then they went up to Dubravica, we saw when he went up to Dubravica after about half an hour he came back and he says, "you are going to go to the school in Dubravica".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you stay in the Dubravica school until 1st May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you put in a room, Ms. Ahmic, with other women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there -- it was a big room there with people, young people, there were a lot of people, a lot of women and children, and I was in a class room with the grandchildren, and those who had small children, they allowed them to be in the class rooms. Then the men, they were all put in a big room, it was all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, were there drawings on the walls in the room where you and the other Muslim women and children were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were drawings, there were such drawings that we could never sleep from, all the terror that was in these drawings. They were putting them up, they were drawing heads and they were writing something and there would be a head drawn and the knife was stuck through like this (indicates) and they said, "this is how we are going to slaughter balijas", and the Muslim women, there would be -- "this is how we would rape Muslim women". I could not read this, but those who could read read it. We spent about ten days in that school building, the Red Cross was enquiring about us and the Red Cross came and found us and then they --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, before you move on in your testimony, let me ask you: what was the reaction of yourself, the other Muslim women and the children to those drawings that were on the walls in the building where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were frightened. Every day we waited to see if they would come and do to us what was on the drawings, every time the door would open we expected something would happen like the things that were drawn on the walls. We were all scared, the children and us. It is terrible, how they were able to draw something like that, what they would do to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The other women who were with you in detention, were those also survivors from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were all from Ahmici, but there were some refugees in Ahmici, down there, and they were in that school building with us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you provided with food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were receiving food, this is what they said. "We kept a few balijas around, so if they want to come and bring some food, fine; if not, you can just croak". They were coming -- we had a little bit of food to give to the children, there was some fish cans and that is what we were giving them. When the Red Cross found out about us, where we were, they brought us biscuits and prepared food in small jars so the children could eat, and my daughter-in-law Suada too. They were coming every morning and they said to go and clean the rooms upstairs, and my daughter-in-law always volunteered because there would be bread up there and then they would bring bread for the children and there was also some margarine. There was also a little bit of jam that was given, that was if you went to clean the rooms, and so they went. I also would go and I looked to see which soldier to ask, to ask for some bread. I would tell him that the children did not have food, to give us some food, because the children were crying. We did not have anything, we had no conditions, and as I said, the children were crying. They were taking the young ones to dig trenches, they were threatening us, they were bringing some kind of letters and they would read it to us, "see what yours have done, you will see, we will come tonight", and then they had too much alcohol, they would drink too much and then they would take women, they would take them to rape them. They would come with flash lights, so at night, they would come, because there was no electricity, so they would take and look for younger women to take them out. I also recognised one of our neighbours, his name was Anto -- wait a minute -- Miskovic. I told him, "Anto, I know you from somewhere. You drank coffee in my yard", and he said, "I also recognise you, you were friendly with my grandmother, but I am ashamed at what these idiots of ours have been doing. If someone comes to look for women, I will be in the room next door, and whoever has the strongest voice should yell and you just yell as hard as you can and I will come over, so do not be afraid". They were coming to the other rooms, they would take them to other rooms and he was sleeping in the room next door, right next door to us and whenever we needed any help, he would help us. There was also another one, he was a young man, 17 or 18 maybe, he was also in the class room where I was and he lost a chain and there was also a cross on this chain and he tells me, he was at the door and he said, "you, the old woman, I want that chain by the dark. You see this knife here?", and he touched himself, "I am going to carve a cross right here" (indicates). My grandchildren started crying, and then again this Anto came in and he said, "what happened?", and I told him, "this young man is telling me, I do not know, he lost some chain and I should produce it for him. If I do not find it, he is going to carve a cross into here, on to my forehead". He again told me, this Anto did, "do not be afraid while I am here". He had a little bit to drink, but I said, "I am afraid of him".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, you left the Dubravica school on 1st May 1993. Were you given an opportunity to return to the summer kitchen in your home, or back into the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No way, there were no houses left, all of the houses burnt down, all of them were in flames, all the Muslim houses were burned down. Not a single one remained intact. You can have a look at those pictures, there is not a single Muslim house left that was not set afire. All of them were set on fire. Where could I go back? They would not let us go back. When the Red Cross came, when they asked us who wanted to go home and who would go where and who had someone in Zenica, some relatives or something, we could only write down that we wanted to go to Zenica or to Travnik, nowhere else. We could not write down Vitez because we did not have anywhere to go in Vitez. They gave us those little cards from the Red Cross and they found buses for us. They took us all to Zenica and then in Zenica, every one of us tried to do his or her best. I said that I wanted to go to the village of Arnauti because I have two of my husband's sisters living there. When I came there, dirty, barefoot, we were there for about 15 days almost and you could not change and you could not wash yourself, and I was standing there like a gypsy over there at the station. I can see myself now the way I looked. My daughter-in-law's uncle came to pick her and the children up and he told me, "come with us", and then my daughter was living as a refugee in Raspotocje and she found out that we had come and she sent a man to bring me over, but she did not know that her father was killed. She sent a man to pick us up and when I got out, she said, "mother, where is father?". I said, "father has been killed, dear", and she went to the door over there in this house where she was staying at Raspotocje and I followed her and that is how it was. You know, the things they did to us, you cannot imagine, you have never seen it even on film, it was horrible, you cannot imagine. They did not pay any attention to whether someone was old or young or ill or a child, they would kill everyone whom they saw, and whoever they would find in houses or in front of houses. I really wonder why they did not kill me. Many women were killed, children were killed. Three month old babies were killed. My sister-in-law, a three month old baby of theirs was killed. Terrible, these things were awful. May God not allow things like that to happen to anyone, the kind of things that we went through in the village of Ahmici. Everything was destroyed, everything was burnt down. We cannot even go there until the present day to see where our homes were, they will not allow us. We would go two or three times to the mosque, but they would send their escort with us, their policemen, somebody wanted to go to their burnt down houses to take something they would find, at least as a memento, a little something from the burnt down houses, but no, they would never allow anyone to do that. They would not allow anyone to stop there at their own houses, only at the mosque, because there were houses nearby near the mosque, but they would never let anyone stop at the houses, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, thank you very much for your testimony. Now General Blaskic's lawyers will have an opportunity to ask you some questions. I have concluded, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Harmon. We will resume at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a trial, there is an accused and he has counsel. The attorneys for General Blaskic will now ask you some questions that they consider proper to ask you. Do you feel a bit rested, are you all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Hello, Ms. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My name is Anto Nobilo and this is my colleague Russell Hayman and we defend General Blaskic. I am sorry that I will be troubling you a bit further, but only with a few questions. You told the Prosecutor that your husband, the late Hasim, went on guard. Who was his commander? Who said when he would go on guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Ramo Bilic, there was Mirsad Ahmic, they are the ones who said who would go and my son also, he said who would go to stand guard. They did not say that they would go to stand guard in order to defend themselves from the Croats, because everybody knew that the Chetniks were threatening us, because they used to go on guard together, the Croats and the Muslims before, but when we were first attacked, then they started separating themselves from us, and they would not allow our people to go on guard with them, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, your late husband Hasim, did he stand guard only in your hamlet, or did he go to Gornji Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he would take the road from the cafe to the road to Ahmici, that was the road where he stood guard. He was an elderly man and they would not let him go further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, your hamlet, is it called Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you are from Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, your son Fahrudin, who was his commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one, they did not have a commander, they did not have any kind of a commander. What kind of a commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You just said -- who told him when he would stand guard, your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one, I do not know who he took his orders from. I do not know. Ahmic -- you know those three brothers who were killed, I cannot remember his name now, his brother was a witness here, Muris Ahmic, so he was the commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, where was their command, where would they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no command at our place, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there something at the elementary school in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some kind of conference at the school, I do not know. I know at the beginning when we were first attacked by the Croats that older Croats and Muslims would meet there in order to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When your son obtained weapons from Slemenje, did other people from the village get some too or was he the only one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, other people too, other people from Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: They all got weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they made new weapons from old ones. Drago personally helped my son make the rifle that he had and Drago's brother-in-law took that rifle away from my son and I gave it to Drago Josipovic. You can ask Drago Josipovic about it and he will tell you it is the truth. They took weapons from all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see weapons being taken from other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They ordered my son, Nenad ordered my son that if arms were not surrendered by 6.00 that they would all be blown up, that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, before, did you make any statements to anyone, did you tell anybody else about all these events before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, when I made a statement, I made this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you first make a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I remember, honey, I have no idea when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it closer to that event? Was it a few years ago, several years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is more than a year since then, it has been more than a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I would like to ask you specifically, what is the purpose of asking three questions to know whether Ms. Ahmic had made a statement. I assume that she did make a statement, you have the right to the statement, you said "in the statement", why are you asking these questions? I do not quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It will be clear from the sequel, your Honour, because I will try to show there is a considerable difference between the previous statements and this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And right now, you have just said what I knew you were going to say. You ask the same questions of each witness, you say you made statements and I have begun to understand, as have my colleagues, in order to get her to see what discrepancies there would be in the statements, there are discrepancies, there would be some, of course, she has the right to make some, we are wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I understand, but I would like to know how soon after the events the statement was made. Was her recollection better then than now? Excuse me, Ms. Ahmic, I have another question to put to you. When you made this first statement, were all these events fresh in your memory or do you remember better today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, how could I not remember when I first made my statement and now, a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But when did you better recollect these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I made my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, I ask my colleague Russell Hayman to read a text in English, he will do it better than I will, and the interpreters will interpret it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Page 2, bottom, and I apologise, your Honour, the copy of the statement we were given is not dated, which required some additional inquiry by Mr. Nobilo. The reference is to 1500 hours on the afternoon before the attack on 16th April 1993: "Kordic was holding a book and threw it on the table and said there will be no more negotiations, only war." This is a reference to the TV programme: "Kordic said HVO soldiers from Bungalow Cafe were attacked in Ahmici. Blaskic was sitting next to Kordic, but I don't remember if he said anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that true what you said then, what you told the investigators then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What did I say? I did not understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will tell you briefly. You said you watched television and that Kordic said that HVO soldiers were attacked in Ahmici at the bungalow and that Kordic said that there would be no more negotiations, only war and that he threw the book, but that Blaskic was sitting next to Kordic and that you do not remember if he said anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I do remember, of course, how could I not remember? Blaskic said the following, Blaskic said, "in the village of Ahmici, our soldiers were attacked at the bungalow", and some other people were sitting there at the table and a woman was there with them. He said, Kordic, he threw this book or paper, he was upset, and he said there would be no more negotiations and no talks, "we are only waiting for our orders and we are going to wage war". We were terrified, my husband and I and my son and whoever watched this on television, and we were attacked the very next morning at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, perhaps you did not hear me well. In your first statement, you said that you do not remember that Blaskic said anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would object. The witness made it clear that she did remember, she remembers today what she saw on television and she has testified about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to get back to the objection, which seems well-founded to me. I want to do some pedagogical work with you, as we do with the Prosecution. I think it would have been much simpler if you had simply said -- let me give you a demonstration, I am not Defence counsel, you know that, but let me tell you, "Ms. Ahmic, let us go back to the famous scene you saw on television, to the Prosecution, Mr. Kordic said this, Mr. Blaskic said that. We have the impression, we the defenders of General Blaskic that you have a scene in your memory which is a bit different from what you said before. Do you agree with that or not?". We would have immediately got to where we want to. Now we are getting into a confused situation in regard of the witness, you said, "you said this, you said that". No, you had the intention to reconstruct what in your eyes were the statements she made previously. As for the Prosecutor's objection, I sustain it because the witness has already answered. It is a question of method I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will ask the question. Ms. Ahmic, you understand, I have explained things very clearly to you, the counsel for General Blaskic are wondering about something you said in your first statement, as to what you heard from Mr. Kordic and what you heard from Mr. Blaskic. For the sake of the Tribunal, could you say very simply, while remembering what you said previously, could you state what it was that Mr. Kordic said and what it was that Mr. Blaskic said and answer the judges directly, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I will always tell you the way I have already put it. General Blaskic said the following, "in the village of Ahmici", he said this in person on television, "in the village of Ahmici, our soldiers were attacked", and Tihomir Blaskic at the same time took something and threw this and he said, "there will be no more negotiations, we are only waiting for our orders and there can only be war". I cannot tell you differently. Until my death if you ask me that, that is what I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. In general, contradictions, Mr. Nobilo, I say this for the Prosecutor as well, contradictions are not fundamental. They may be important when things have been said two, three, four years ago. What I think is of interest to the Tribunal is what the witness is saying today. Of course the statements that she made are important, because I understand that you have based your whole Defence on the written statements which were given to you and that you are pointing them out as you go along, I think that is your right, but you must understand that today, this is a verbal procedure and the witness is looking at the judges, the judges are looking at the witness. Go ahead, please. Judge Riad would like to state something as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please try to be more precise. You said that General Blaskic said, "you are going to be attacked at the bungalow", and then who threw the paper and said, "there will be war". Was it Blaskic too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It was Kordic who threw the paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kordic through the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he say there would be war or there would be a massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We are only waiting for our orders", they attacked us in the morning and there was a massacre. We were massacred in the most terrible way. Please, gentlemen, I remember the previous war, I was nine years old, but what happened this time in the village of Ahmici, may it not be repeated ever again. They killed everyone, the young and the old, and it is not that there was some kind of army that could defend us, it is not that someone could come to our aid, they destroyed everything, houses, women, children. In two or three hours they destroyed everything that we had been building up throughout our life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Ahmic, I believe that you answered the judge's questions, he is satisfied with your answer, there will be some other questions that the judges will ask you later on, but for the time being, I give the floor back to Mr. Nobilo so that he can continue the questions he wishes to ask. Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Ms. Ahmic, we are now coming to the part when Drago and Miro walked up to you and offered their condolences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was during the first fighting, when we were first attacked, when we were first attacked. There was six months between these two attacks, when we were first attacked and the next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how to talk that way. I just know that there were six months between these two attacks on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did this conversation take place? Was it when your late Fahrudin was killed or was it earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please explain this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Drago and Miro Josipovic walked up to you and offered their condolences on the occasion of the death of your son.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was during the second attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the first time when you made a statement, you said that you do not need their condolences and they replied that they could not save him because they were afraid. That is what you said when you first testified. Today you said that the killing was ordered by a higher force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said, "Drago, the murderers who killed my son came from your yard, you know who killed my son", he said, "do not ask me, it is a higher force that ordered this". That is what he told me. This was after he offered me his condolences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is this the same thing that you told the investigators before when they asked you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did. That is exactly what happened. I think that is what I said. But for me, six months and then a year, a year has gone by since I made my statement, I do not remember, you know sometimes I really get lost. Since this has happened to me, I am losing my memory, I walk into the house, for example, into the room and I start wondering why I walked into the house, you know, when all these pictures come before my eyes, all the things I have suffered, I wonder --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it worse for you now or was it worse for you before? How do you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same for me. As I loved my child when I had him, I love him all the same and it is more difficult for me now when my grandchildren, Fahrudin's children, when they hurt my old wounds again. Less than a month ago, Emir, my youngest grandson, he lives in Zenica, he walked up to me and he said, "grandma, I saw a man, he looked just like my father, he had hair like my father and a jacket like my father, everything like my father and I hid behind a house and I shouted 'father' and he turned around". Can you imagine how this little boy, his son, sees things? This is his youngest son and he keeps seeing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I wish to draw your attention to your conversation with Nikica Slikica, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During your first conversation with the investigators, you said that you asked Nikica to tell you what happened, and Nikica said, "do not look for them any more, they are dead, it is better for you not to know where they are".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that, that is not what I said. I called him over nicely and I said, "Nikica, please come here", and he said, "now what do you want?" That is what he told me. I said, "Nikica, please come over and tell me, where did they take the four of them?", and he said "some kind of exchange". I said, "Nikica, please swear by your dead mother, Mara, who was a friend of mine, tell me the truth, do not hide anything from me", and then he said, "look, if you are asking me to swear by my dead mother, Mara, although she is dead, she means a lot for me; orders came and they were killed, so now they are killed".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that what you told the investigators the first time when you made a statement? Did you use the same words to describe this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I described it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know these other women, they were brought from the other surrounding villages, younger women, they came with torch lights and they were looking for younger women and they would throw light on every woman and they wanted to see who they liked and then they would take them away. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacetd). We women, we were prisoners and we were not allowed to meet with each other. Later on we were told they would use torch lights and come looking for these younger women, etcetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see this or did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there for 15 days, how would we not hear it? We would hear them, they would drink beer all night and they would yell, "we are going to look for balija women, ones that suit us". This Anto I told you about, I forgot his name again --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miskovic, two or three days earlier, my son went to Vujica's for cevapi, with his wife and this Anto came and he was with him. When he saw my daughter-in-law, when he asked, "are you Fahrudin's wife?", and she said yes and he said, "it is impossible that you look that way", she had changed so much during three days, she was changed beyond recognition, she looked five years older after all this suffering she had gone through and after having seen her husband killed. Also his three children and his wife saw my son being killed, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and also did they come to your room to look for women with a torch light?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would come but they did not like any of the women here. They said, "fuck these women, it is only old women. We do not want them".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am just going to refer to an earlier statement of yours and I am going to ask my colleague Russell to read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
