utterances.text: I was first to come out, I unlocked the door and the moment I stepped out, I saw everything. I saw Sabahudin Zec lying killed in front of our house and his wife Hajrija with a small girl was close by. I saw a soldier, two of their soldiers who were standing in the road, and somebody was lying by them. That was Adnan Zec who was wounded. I saw Mirsad's house on fire, as well as Husein's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you right there and ask you, you saw Husein Ahmic's house on fire, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How soon after you had seen Husein Ahmic murdered by these soldiers was it that you saw his house on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many minutes was it between the time you saw Husein Ahmic murdered and the time you saw his house on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was your other neighbour's house on fire as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that neighbour a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Husein Ahmic likewise was a Muslim, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You also testified that you saw certain members of the Zec family who were dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify the members of the Zec family by name who you saw were dead, and their ages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sabahudin Zec, around 45. His wife, Hajrija Zec and little Melisa, who was 6 or 7. The son Adnan, he was 15, he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were these bodies in relation to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Zecs? The bodies were in front of our house in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How far away from them were you when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right in front of our house, the house where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How old was -- you said you saw a boy by the name of Adnan Zec, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he alive or was he dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was unconscious at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know his age?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there soldiers next to the Zec family members who you have just identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers standing by the members of the Zec family who you have just identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, two were standing near Adnan and two approached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were those soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They also wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One last question about the Zec family; were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you came out on to the front of your house, what happened next? What did you do and what did members of your family do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I unlocked the door, then they told us to surrender. All four of us surrendered and the two of us who threw in the hand grenade separated my husband from us. We continued down the road and I do not know anything about him. I heard two or three bullets and I went away with my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How soon after you separated from your husband was it that you heard the shots, the bullet shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you passed by 30 metres and then you heard shots, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did not allow us to turn around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you ever seen your husband since April 16th 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never again, neither dead or alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did the soldiers tell you to do? Did they tell you to leave the house? Where did they tell you to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To run up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where was "there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear what the soldiers told the family members, the surviving family members of Husein Ahmic's family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they expelled Samira and her two small children. They did not even allow her to put socks on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your landlord on April 16th 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he is also missing, just like my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the house that you occupied on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They set it on fire and everything burnt down in one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We know because we were told by the people from Gornji Ahmici who watched it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Husein Ahmic have a son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Munir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Munir escaped through the bathroom window towards his -- in the direction of his brother's Nedzib's house and he was then wounded and the UNPROFOR took him to the hospital in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness I, what did you do after you fled your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Nezir Ahmic's house. He asked me about my husband, I said I did not know, that the two men had separated him from us. He told me to stay with him and I said that I did not dare wait for them there, because I saw what they were doing, and the children led me, because I could barely walk because I had lost my strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were fleeing from your house, did you have an opportunity at all to look back on to the part of lower Ahmici? Did you see what was happening to the other houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all houses were in flames. They took over everything at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you go that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went up towards upper Ahmici, to a woman, and she gave me a pill and she gave me a blanket and she gave something to my daughter to put on her feet because she had left barefoot. Then we were given some coffee and some food, then we waited until 11.00, then we went towards the village of Vrhovine. We finally made it there by 1.00. We were there until about 4.00 and then a man from there said, "whoever wants to go to Zenica should go, and the rest will stay, but it is better to go because there will be shells coming", and 40 shells were lobbed in there. I went to Zenica because I had nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness I, let me clarify one part of your testimony, and that is the part when you described seeing the Zec family. Do you know how many girls were in the Zec family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was another one and she survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the girl who survived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, one was Elisa, one was Melisa, and I do not know which one was killed and which one survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April 1993, do you know the ages of those two girls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the name of the surviving one, but it was the little one, the smallest one was the one who was actually killed. She was 6 to 7, the little one, and maybe they were a year apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded my questions of this witness. I would request that we go into a closed session for a matter of just a few minutes because I would like to tender some exhibits that would possibly indirectly identify this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will ask the Registrar to have us go into closed session. Are you going to show some photographs for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, individuals, Mr. President. A picture of a house and a picture of a portion of Exhibit 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. So we are talking about a private session then, not a closed session, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Private session is fine, Mr. President. The exhibits will be in the possession of counsel and your Honours, so that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 4050 redated - in closed session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness I, my name is Anto Nobilo and together with my colleague Mr. Hayman, we defend General Blaskic. I am going to put one or two questions at the most to you. Do you know how many families together with you came from Karaula to Ahmici as refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a lot of us, but I do not know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any refugees from Jajce, Prijedor, Mr.konjic Grad and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever see General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I now turn to my colleagues. Judge Riad, have you a question you would like to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I shall call you Witness I, I shall not say your name. Among the things you related was the killing of the members of the Zec family, and among them was little Melisa, who was six years old and Adnan, 15 years old, apart from Sabahudin and his wife and all that. Who killed them, do you know? Were they killed by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean the soldiers killed a little child, six years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did it happen in other families too that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they even killed younger children, three months old, three months and three days old in a cradle, babies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: By shooting them or by burning them or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would shoot them and they would burn them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness I, we have finished, you have been very courageous, the Tribunal extends many thanks to you. We will suspend the session now, we will ask the witness to remain seated and we will resume in about 15 minutes. We are now suspending the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are now resuming the hearing. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in respect of the previous witness, Witness I, I failed to move to admit Prosecutor's Exhibit 131 and I would do so at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections from the Defence, but it seems to me, I think, that we are going to bring the whole court back just in order to point that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I did not ask the court to come back in order to introduce that exhibit. We have concluded today, Mr. President. We anticipated we would have a full day with three witnesses and we finished some minutes short. I apologise, but those were the witnesses who were available and prepared to testify today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No more witnesses now. Since we have a few minutes to talk, before we adjourn the hearing, how do things look for the rest of this week and next week? I would like to recall that, for the judges, there is no hearing tomorrow. We will resume on Thursday and Friday and then next week, it will be a regular week, except for Friday, which I think is the 28th. We will not be meeting on the 28th, except for in the morning where we have scheduled a status conference. Mr. Harmon, what do things look like for the rest of the week here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in respect of the remainder of the week we have three witnesses scheduled for Thursday. We have forward planning where we identify witnesses two weeks in advance for ourselves and for the Victims and Witnesses Unit. This week, we have had some difficulties, Mr. President. We have had two witnesses we have identified who will not be able to appear, and we are in the process of attempting to essentially find additional witnesses. We have witnesses coming in for the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand. These are tragic events, I do not want to make any jokes about this here, but why are you -- it seems a little strange to me to say, "we did not have the witnesses who could come, so we will try to find some other ones". That should not be necessary, should it? It seems a bit strange for me to hear that. I hope you do not mind my saying that to you, I say it in a friendly way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I did not intend it in perhaps the way the court understood it. What I mean to say is we have witnesses coming in for the following week's session. We anticipate the hearing on Friday, but at this point in time find ourselves in a situation where witnesses who we anticipated would appear on Friday are unable to appear, and if the court desires the session to proceed, then the witnesses who we have summoned for the following week we anticipate will be arriving on Thursday evening, and we could endeavour to prepare some witnesses who would be arriving on Thursday night for testimony on Friday morning, if the court so desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When will we know that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the flights -- we are advised on Thursday night whether the flights have arrived successfully here in The Hague. Sometimes they are delayed for reasons that are beyond our control, and that has happened once in this case where a flight was delayed, it arrived very, very late at night and we had to prepare witnesses for the following morning, so we anticipate it will arrive on Thursday evening at this point in time, subject to the weather in that part of the world, and any other potential problems dealing with the timely arrival of flights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So one could then suppose that if there are no witnesses on Friday, would both the Defence and Prosecution be prepared to have the status conference then, instead of on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On behalf of the Prosecution, Mr. President, we would be prepared to have that status conference on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We will be filing tomorrow, your Honour, a short reply brief on the hearsay matter and I intend to file by Friday a short reply brief on the matter of source and authenticity. If those briefs need to be before the court, then we would suggest that those matters be addressed at a later date. We could certainly go ahead with all other matters on Friday, and hopefully we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not sure I quite understood. Perhaps I am not understanding correctly. Are you saying that you are supposed to file two additional briefs on the hearsay and on the exculpatory matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we filed a standing objection to hearsay, and a motion concerning source. The Prosecution has filed a response to both of those filings, and I intend to file short replies to both of their responses this week. I think it would be helpful -- those will be short, five pages or less, I think it will be helpful for the court to have those before those matters are heard. We certainly would be prepared to address all other matters at a status conference on Friday. We would hope, if we do that, that we could recapture the 28th as a trial day, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We cannot have the whole day for the 28th, it can only be in the morning, which is why we decided there would be a status conference, that we would not therefore meet on the afternoon of the 28th. Now I am coming back to the two questions of the hearsay and the sources. You are expecting to file short responses, I am asking the Prosecution and the Defence, do you want these two issues to be argued before the Tribunal or do you want a response only to the briefs that you will have filed, including those tomorrow, or do you prefer that this be argued? Because if it needs to be argued, I can tell you then your briefs first have to be received, and we have to wait for the translation into French, which means that it would not be argued before December. But we have to have the agreement of our parties. Do you wish to argue or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, our filing on hearsay was not styled in the nature of a motion, it was a standing objection. If the court accepts that standing objection, in that form, we do not feel the need for a hearing, unless it would be helpful to the court. I can say with respect to the matter of source and authenticity, it might well be helpful to orally address that matter before the court. Again, I think that is within the court's discretion. The court is never compelled in a matter such as this to hold a hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that I can speak for my colleagues. My idea was to try to gain some time, which would mean that if this argument is going to take up witness time -- Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in respect of both of those pleadings, the Prosecutor is prepared to submit our position on the written submissions to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Our first choice, your Honour, would be to have trial on Friday. If there is a witness here and the Prosecution can make adequate preparation, let us use the day, because the court's trial time is the most precious resource we all have. We wish to conserve it to the highest degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you are speaking now about this Friday, Friday of this week, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Friday 21st, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So if I have understood, we cannot take a decision at this very moment, but we will leave things stand as they are. So (i), everybody's preference is that we have witnesses on Friday; (ii) that the status conference would be ready, unless we bring up the issue of hearsay evidence, but the point of the status conference was to see where we are in this Blaskic trial and having to do with the two issues I would like us to try to gain some time and that the Tribunal will see in light of the applications and responses on both sides, we will decide then at least for the hearsay, we might not need to have pleadings,. But if you wish, or rather if the Tribunal decides that we should have pleadings, that this will be taking witness time up and then the Tribunal will ask you to be brief in your arguments, because we will have all the written documents for us to reach a decision. On that note, we will adjourn until the day after tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Thursday, 20th October 1997)
